t: Bowing to a Voice of One
q: Good leaders listen to this feedback and take it to heart. They examine what occurred and why it produced such a negative reaction.
In an audience of 100 people, how much weight should a leader place on a single voice? In some cases, a lot. In other cases, not much.
They attempt to triangulate with others what could have possibly led to such a complaint.
The danger of allowing a lone voice to influence future meetings and events is to become overly guarded and to dilute the elements that make for lively discussions.
A vanilla approach that hopefully satisfies everyone equates to giving up and giving in to the tyranny of one.

t: #74 Ask an Impossible Question to Further Check Students' Understanding
q: The students will not be taught trigonometry for a few years, so the question was impossible to answer with the tools at their disposal. And that is what made it such a good check for understanding.
The teacher made this even more effective by not saying anything. She just popped it up on the board, just like she had done for every other question that lesson.
I have seen teachers use similar unanswerable questions, but sugar-coat them with hints such as Think carefully about this one, or Are we sure we can answer this one?

I have written previously about the problem with offering unavoidable hints - they reduce the validity of the check for understanding, and rob students of the opportunity to think hard and show what they really can do.
By offering no such hints, the teacher had an accurate sense of what students knew and didn't know, and the subsequent mini-whiteboard check dew out some interesting misconceptions.
So, now and then, throw in an impossible question, but disguise the fact that it is impossible.

t: Everything Bagel Leaders
q: Their inability to say No creates an unnecessary burden on the team that often leads to exhaustion, frazzle, and burnout.
There is nothing worth saying No to if you’re an Everything Bagel Leader. Ideas and projects arrive in a never-ending wave.
The Everything Bagel Leader will never accept this re-prioritization, so team members ask for forgiveness later rather than permission, as the saying goes.
A leader who always says Yes can be a curse for a productive team.
Turning 10 priorities into three is how good team members survive.

t: How To Handle A Disruptive Autistic Student
q: I’m not an expert in autism. Nor do I have a degree or teaching credential in special education. I write only from the perspective of a classroom teacher.
I believe that the SCM approach—with its focus on responsibility, intrinsic motivation, pursuit of excellence, and kindness and respect—is best for all students.
It’s not you and your individual interventions that make the difference. It’s the SCM classroom climate and culture itself that is most impactful and best helps each student improve.

An autistic student only disrupts the class if you and your students are disrupted. In other words, as long as the class is well-behaved and on-task, then a calling out or other noise is just that. Keep teaching. Let it go. It’s okay and your class will understand.

If the student continues to act dangerously—running out of the room, climbing on cabinets, hitting others, etc.—then you must call for help, document the behavior, and then seek direction from your principal.

If your administration ignores you and you’re being hung out to dry, then you should consider changing schools. Really. If you can’t ensure your own safety and that of your students, then you need to get out of there.
The overarching answer to autistic students who may not be able to follow rules is compassion combined with excellent all-class classroom management. It can do wonders when applied day after day.

t: A Great Attitude Without the Discipline to Excel
q: Discipline is THE moderating factor between will and skill, and team members with a positive attitude who underperform often lack it.
It usually isn’t because they can’t learn or master the skills that will make them successful. It’s because they lack the discipline to take the daily steps necessary to acquire those skills.
Now for the bad news: leaders can’t teach attitude or instill discipline in others. These are decisions and practices only the team member can infuse in themselves.
Discipline is the bridge between goals and accomplishment. The desire to excel often exists independently from the focus, organization, and consistency discipline provides.
A great attitude is only a game-changer if it comes with the self-discipline to make the daily actions connected to success.

t: Refraining From Unilateral Decisions Applies to Everyone on the Team, Not Just Leaders
q: Wise leaders do their best to make and keep the promise that they will not make unilateral decisions that affect others without first seeking their input.
Team members are more likely to stay put when they follow a leader who refrains from making unilateral decisions.
If they are “thinking” of leaving the team, the leader would like to learn about it before a final decision is made.
Leaders who refrain from making unliteral decisions that affect team members have every right to ask for reciprocity.
When leaders AND team members refrain from unilateral decision-making, a higher and more reciprocal trust is shared by everyone on the team.

t: Accolades for Team Members Not Yet Ready for Prime Time Foster Team Cohesion
q: There is no such thing as an insignificant team member on a highly cohesive team. The team wins or loses as a unit, not as a collection of stars and reserves.
Too often, results-oriented leaders and coaches give attention, time, and accolades exclusively to their top performers.
The best leaders and coaches look for reasons to recognize and acknowledge those behind the “starting” unit.
Leaders who frequently give accolades to those “riding the bench” foster a different team mentality than do others.
This places a check on the egos of those on the stage and reminds them that they succeed when everyone else on the team does as well.

t: The Truth Is More Palatable When We Discover It for Ourselves
q: No matter how self-aware a person is, we cling to our perceptions and seek confirmation to validate our views.
When people discover such truths for themselves, they internalize the feedback in a way no leader can replicate by telling or showing them.
Provocative questions that ask others to critically examine their views are best left to linger without the leader addressing them.
Once the question takes hold, it has its own influence without the need for much discussion.
The truth can only be tolerated when you discover it for yourself, because then the pride of discovery makes it palatable.

t: Inside Every Complaint Is a Request
q: Buried inside the complaint is a request for change or resolution. We complain in the hope that others will do things differently to address our discontent.
Listening to people complain is akin to hearing a cat’s screech. Complaints make us uncomfortable, defensive, and anxious.
They remind themselves and others that inside every complaint lies a request for change. Hence, they ask people to make the request instead of the complaint.
Complaining that the parachute didn’t open is never as smart as requesting the parachute packers do a great job.
People respond much better to requests for change than they do complaints for change.

t: You Might Be a Micromanager If
q: The comedian Jeff Foxworthy delighted his fans in the 1990s with a never-ending string of one-liners about how to tell if they might be a redneck.
Micromanagers dictate and control nearly every move of those they lead and manage.
Their controlling nature robs team members of the independent action, risk-taking, and creative problem-solving essential for personal development.
You might be a micromanager if the frequency with which you check on the progress of an assignment is best measured in seconds and minutes.
You might be a micromanager if the team has created a special therapy group to work through their issues with your leadership style.

t: Star Teammates Dont Fall From the Sky
q: Not everyone can be a star performer, but anyone can be a star teammate.
A great team member owns every problem faced by the team as their own, and they take responsibility for addressing it.
They don’t wait to be asked to chip in or to contribute. They show up and get to work, completing their own tasks while scanning the horizon for team challenges.
Their star power is not about advanced skill or acumen, but rather arises from their emergent leadership and their unrelenting desire to make the team better.
They don’t exist without the support of leaders who view them as an asset and not competition.

t: Shame
q: Ms C cringes visibly. Now, most of us have heard about how learning styles are a myth and not useful when thinking of learning in the classroom.
With Ms J, she could not hide her disdain but with her students, there was more understanding.
It is highly likely she was told about learning styles and dual coding in a CPD session with very little in terms of a follow-up or reflection.
I am not trying to make Ms J out to be someone who isn’t intelligent enough or resourceful. I have been a version of Ms J.
But I have also been a version of Ms C and been judgemental of others who still hold views I used to and that I feel have been proven wrong.
We need to stop shaming those we perceive to believe the ‘wrong’ things. And we need to stop feeling ashamed if we need to change our views and learn.

t: September Routines
q: No matter how much preparation work I do over the summer holidays, the first two weeks of September always feel insanely busy and stressful.
It's important to set behaviour expectations at the start of the year with every class, not just with new Year 7s.
I decided to wait a couple of weeks to launch this because students already experience information overload at the start of the year.
This seems like an obvious thing to say, but I know that many schools don't do it: I think it's vital to relaunch your homework platform every year.
Admittedly these letters are rather long so I know that some parents won't read them, but I do always get some parents thanking me for providing the information upfront.

The letters cover all the frequently asked questions... which will (hopefully) reduce workload for my team throughout the year because teachers won't get individual emails from parents asking about these things.

t: Organizations Dont Learn People Inside of Them Do
q: As a result, we often wait for and expect the organization to learn from its mistakes and successes.
But the reality is that organizations don’t learn. People do.
This is why it is so important to institutionalize the working knowledge of its most experienced practitioners.
Sustaining knowledge and wisdom relies on leaders repetitively sharing what they know throughout an organization.
Without a dedicated effort to institutionalize the wisdom of existing leaders, when those people leave or retire, their knowledge goes with them.

t: Cognitive Coaching: Changing Minds and Changing Practice
q: knowledge/experience -> judgement -> action. I think we are pretty good at helping teachers build knowledge... but I don't think we are good (yet) at supporting teachers to develop their judgement.
It also strikes me that if we skip the 'judgement' part of teaching, we are ignoring the very thing that makes a teacher a professional.
Mental models are a construct. Put very simply, they are our knowledge of 'how things work.' They simplify complex situations enabling us to interpret them and act.
Everyone's mental models are different even about similar, simple things, like trees.
Because mental models contain causal relationships, they can be simulated, i.e. we can press play and 'run' what might happen if we do something.

Our mental models are tacit. It's rare we actually examine our mental models rather than just think with them. This is why it's so important for coaches to focus their work on helping the teacher surface their mental models.
Expertise is the ability to do the thing that works most of the time and to know when and how to adapt. It's about recognising 'decision points.'

t: 3-Read Friday #46: Changing Minds, Shame, and Routines
q: Sarah is one of my favourite thinkers, and judging by this debut post, her new newsletter will be a must-read.
Sign up for regular reflections on improving CPD, especially coaching.
Jo contrasts how a teacher might react to a colleague's misconception with how they might react to a misconception held by one of their students.
This really made me reflect on my own perceptions and actions.
Jo describes the routines she employs inside lessons, and for things like homework, student support and parental communication.

t: What Does It Mean to Be Fully Prepared
q: We don’t consider ourselves prepared for any event, situation, or upcoming performance until we establish the goals we want to achieve and have settled on the strategy and tactics that will enable us to succeed.
Their preparation includes knowing and understanding whatever information or facts they will need to rely on in order to succeed.
Being fully prepared also includes pre-deciding the best course of action in case things don’t go as planned.
What is less known about skilled preparation is the benefit many performers derive from visualization.
Until you can “see” what you want to have happen and the steps you need to execute to achieve your goals, you’re not completely prepared.

t: The Problem With Project-Based Learning
q: It was a brilliant look at how weather affected the performance of different sizes and configurations of rockets he’d made in his garage.
You see, Seth did the project all by himself. And it showed. His tri-fold display board had all the earmarks of a nine-year-old boy—uneven scissor cuts, finger smudges, and remnants of crusted glue.

Presumably, the winning students did help with their projects. But amid all the attention they got that evening—the proud smiles, applause, photos, and balloons—it was hard not to be discouraged. The whole affair was farcical.
Allowing anyone other than students to play an active role in project-based learning is a bad idea. It’s unfair. It’s dishonest. It’s discriminatory toward students who do the work themselves.
Furthermore, they know they didn’t actually do the work, which can destroy their self-worth and leave them afraid to try anything on their own.

Be willing to disallow, require a redo, or remove points for any part of a project that was clearly done by an adult or pulled right off the internet. If you observe the work closely, and look out for it, it’s easy to tell.
You best honor your students not with a meaningless, unearned certificate destined for a box in the family attic, but with skills and abilities that continue to impact them far into the future.

t: As a Last Resort, Consider Exclusion to Reinvigorate a Wayward Team Member
q: Team members sometimes act defiantly when they are protected by bureaucracy, a senior mentor, a critical client relationship, or deep institutional knowledge.
Unfortunately, appealing to the good nature of such a team member often empowers them to be even more resistant and hostile to playing along.
Perhaps nothing is more coercive to a team member than excluding them from the team.
As time goes on, the power of being a social being, first and foremost, sometimes takes precedence.
As a catalyst for resetting a rebellious and obstinate team member, exclusion offers a unique strategy that can sometimes work wonders.

t: Tips for Starting Pop-Up Debates Well
q: One of my classes is seventh grade social studies, and this will be my first year to try pop-up debates. I'm going to start by just calling it a pop-up the first few times, kind of like a game.
Once I get them used to popping up with super short phrases, I'll move on to full sentences from a sentence stem. I'm really excited to use this in my classroom!
She's aware of the initial hurdle: kids' anxiety about public speaking. To help her students overcome this hurdle, she's doing a few smart things.
While Connie's approach to helping kids over that public speaking anxiety hurdle is different from mine, I gotta tell ya, colleague: I like hers more.
Why? Because it's hers. Because it's smart. Because she's excited about it. And because it's going to work.

I pulled this student aside, explained Pop-Up Debates, and told the student they are invited to participate but not required to do so. I'm hoping that, before the semester is through, this student will experience the success of standing up during a PUD.

t: Those Who Coach Others Are More Receptive to Feedback
q: Developing the talents, skills, and knowledge of team members is not a solo act for team leaders.
They quickly learn that those who coach others are more receptive to the coaching efforts of the leader.
By serving in the role of coach for a colleague, they naturally reevaluate the purpose of criticism and how important it is for improving performance.
Leaders constantly dole out these assignments, making sure not to overlook the possibility of reverse mentoring where juniors assist seniors in areas of their know-how and strength.
Peers coaching peers unleashes a learning and performance mindset in a more powerful way than any one leader could achieve on their own.

t: #72 After a Cold Call Write the Student's Answer on the Board
q: In newsletter #17, I wrote about giving students enough time to think after hearing another student’s answer.
All too often, teachers respond immediately to a student’s answer, either saying it is correct or not, or asking another student what they think of the answer.
A way to combat this urge is to write students’ answers on the board after they have said them.

Instead of making your next move (for example, telling Molly she is incorrect, asking another student what they think, or instigating a Turn and Talk), you first write Molly’s answer on the board, nice and big so everyone can see.
The three seconds this takes are vital to give your students and yourself time to process Molly’s answer.
Hence, it acts as a frame of reference for whatever move you make next, avoiding falling victim to the transient information effect.

t: Leaders Spread Behaviors Like Germs
q: Mirror neurons in the brain allow us to realistically simulate the actions performed by others and the results they experience.
We catch and mimic the emotions of others quite easily. Emotions are highly contagious and commonly lead to shared experiences and reactions.
Team members are heavily influenced by what leaders do, not just by what they say or suggest.
Leaders are always on stage for the smallest things they do.
They remind themselves daily that their behaviors spread like fast-growing roots on the tree of imitation.

t: Leaders Can Carry Too Much Truth Through Humor
q: There is a nugget of truth inside every joke or attempt at humor, at least in the mind of the teller.
Humor is a back door, an escape hatch, a source of plausible deniability, a way to insult without being caught red-handed.
They can always tell others they “were only kidding” to escape their obvious guilt.
While there is nothing wrong with an occasional tease or attempt at humor to carry a critical message, leaders who overuse this style often make others paranoid as they wait for the next “zinger.
As any comedian will tell you, a joke is a deadly serious thing.

t: Establishing a New Team Norm
q: The unwritten rules that guide team interaction are more powerful than most leaders realize.
Good leaders don’t take the powerful influence of norms for granted.
It is not uncommon for leaders to use a recent bad or negative team episode to illustrate the need for the new norm.
The best norms are not guidelines, rules, or principles, but specific behaviors that leaders and team members can learn and enact.
The best leaders introduce new norms one at a time, waiting patiently for the new behavior to take hold before initiating another one.

t: Artificial Intelligence Cannot Plan
q: AI can plan your lessons, saving you time and easing your workload. Except it won't, because it can't, because planning is a human process that only happens in human minds.
Those that think AI can plan make an important category error because they don’t understand what planning really is and have confused it with creating resources, which AI is very good at.
Planning is a teacher thinking about the material and how best this can be taught to a particular real life flesh-and-blood class. AI cannot do this.
Tasks and activities that made intuitive sense to the person making the resource made far less sense to a different person because they lack nuance on how each slide should be introduced and framed.
AI is so problematic because it allows the products of planning, resources and timed sequencing, to be produced with minimal thought.
Everything I have ever known in twenty-years working in education convinces me when something is taken away from us it is always replaced by something else.

t: Are Some Students Smarter Than Others?
q: That sentence hung in the air. The implication was clear: maybe we should give up. The student wasn't in special education.

Does intelligence matter? In short, yes. Scoring higher on tests like IQ is correlated with lots of positive things, like lifetime earnings, educational attainment, lack of involvement with the criminal justice system, and more.
Crystallized intelligence is the name for all of the knowledge, skills, and experiences that help us to navigate the world.
It’s helpful for teachers to think in terms of crystallized intelligence, processing speed, and working memory, rather than “smart.

A number of studies suggest that when teachers break skills down into small, manageable parts, teach those parts one at a time, and systematically build up to bigger and bigger ideas, differences in learning speed are narrower.
Knowledge in long-term memory, crystallized intelligence, reduces demands on working memory and processing speed. We think faster when we draw on stuff we know.
Too many students feel dumb in school. They feel like the learning moves too fast, they never seem to get it before the class moves on, and they’re struggling to stay afloat.

t: 3-Read Friday #45: Reading, AI, and Intelligence
q: With a 5-year-old and a 2-year-old at home, I am obsessed with the process of learning to read.
And there is no one better at distilling both theory and practice than Chris.
I recently kicked off a trilogy of posts looking at AI's role in supporting teachers' planning, so I read Ben's post with interest.
I think I am more optimistic than he is, but the point about all the other innovations that were supposed to save teachers time really hit home.
If you fancy a solid overview of intelligence research and its implications for teaching - and who wouldn't? - Dylan's article is excellent.

t: When To Reteach A Routine
q: So when should you reteach a routine? When most of your students are off-track at the same time and thus you’re unable to hold them individually accountable.
It bears mentioning that the second you notice your class going off the rails, it’s best to send them back to their seats or the previous transition to repeat the routine.
An overall sloppy or bad routine, however, is on you because it proves there is something your class isn’t understanding.
Regardless of what it is, the way to correct it is to reteach the routine in greater detail. It doesn’t matter the grade level.
To have a well-behaved and high-achieving class in this day and age you must establish and maintain a culture of excellence that pervades every moment of the school day.

t: Using MGCs to Stoke Student Work Ethic
q: My whole methodology of student motivation was born out of a simple reality: students can only grow toward mastery if they 1) do work, and 2) do it with care.

Paden, I'm noticing that you're not working on the article. Is everything okay? What's getting in your way? Is there anything I can do to help? I'm having this conversation with you because I have high expectations, and I know you can reach them.

By this point in the school year (week 4), being pulled into the hallway for a brief MGC has been normalized. Students know that everyone gets pulled out, and the word on the street is that it can be a simple check-in.

MGCs aren't always possible for all kids at all times. This is a slow-and-steady strategy that reaps its fruits when we use it for one, two, or three kids a day, keeping track to make sure all kids get a moment every month or so.

Kaylin, when you ask those great questions during our article work, I've got to tell you: it is awesome. You're leading the charge of curiosity in this class, and the results of your questions are almost always more questions.
It's really important to look for these last kinds of MGCs because they feel amazing to both the student and to us teachers. Energy boosts all around — good stuff.

t: Great Leaders Know When to Follow
q: A critically important moment in any team occurs when a leader is wise enough to know that they need to follow instead of lead on an issue or initiative.
The humility, confidence, and self-awareness that becoming a follower projects serve to elevate the leader’s credibility and create a trusted bond with the team.
No leader possesses the deepest knowledge, skill, and expertise about all issues and topics.
Leaders who believe a lack of authority prevents them from being effective need to rethink their understanding of leadership.
Followers will always be more important to leaders than leaders are to followers.

t: Tell Your Leader When Youre About to Disagree With Them
q: Weak leaders have a difficult time when a team member has the “audacity” to disagree with them.
But, weak or strong, leaders don’t like to be surprised by disagreement from a team member or colleague.
The most effective team members forecast when they are about to disagree with their leader before making the details of their opposition known.
Less secure leaders are particularly face-sensitive to disagreement about their positions in the presence of others.
Leaders appreciate this advanced notification and think more highly of those who do it.

t: The More We Get Rejected, the More We Succeed
q: Not everyone is going to like, buy, or accept what you promote. Rejection is inevitable.
Wallowing in the bitter taste of rejection simply undermines confidence and results in less risk-taking in the future.
They focus on the opportunity and the chance to compete instead of how much it stings.
They know the real lesson in rejection is not to do less, but to do more.
They view rejection as a necessary precursor to their success.

t: Teacher Transformation: The Two Things It Takes
q: What a good professional development endeavor does: it enables transformation. We don't come to PD hoping to leave entirely unchanged; at the same time, we don't come hoping to change everything.
Well, first, let's be clear: teacher PD can't transform a teacher. Rather, the teacher must do certain kinds of things, with care.
The human mind is constantly renewing itself — dismantling unused things, adopting new things, creating new neural pathways, overwriting old ones.
These aren't just pretty graphics or gimmicks; they are instead graphic organizers for fundamental truths about teaching and learning.
You can watch every YouTube video I've made and read every book I've written 100 times, but if you don't DO THINGS, you won't be transformed. Nor will I.
But theories are only burdensome things when they don't make sense in my mind and don't seem actionable with my body. When theories do meet these criteria, they are a boon.

t: Do You Need to Change the Culture Before Changing the Strategy
q: If the current culture doesn’t align with and support the strategy, the odds the strategy will be successful drop rapidly.
It really doesn’t matter where a sailboat is headed if the wind is not in support. The same is true with the connection between strategy and culture.
When the beliefs, values, and everyday practices of an organization do not align with the strategy, team members will have an impossible time accepting and executing the plan.
Even micro interventions, such as new team norms, can help to reshape the culture and give the strategy a better glide path.
The best leaders don’t talk about the need to change the culture to set the groundwork for a new strategy. When a misalignment exists, they simply go to work.

t: #71 Lower the Content Demands When Introducing a New Routine
q: When routines are unfamiliar, students have to dedicate a large proportion of their limited attention to the routine's structure - in other words, the rules of the routine.
This leaves little attention to think about the content of the routine - the things you actually want them to be thinking about to help them learn.
Using an unfamiliar routine as a vehicle to ask students to think hard about tricky content will achieve little, as neither the structure nor the content will receive sufficient attention.

To develop the routine for responding on mini-whiteboards, initially ask students to write their favourite food or their name, hover and show you, instead of asking them to write the answer to a quadratic equation.
Practising with low content demands is a fast-track towards routine automation.
When the routine is familair, students only need to give minimal attention to the structure and can dedicate their remaining attention to the content.

t: Why We Resist Demand and Commands
q: It’s amazing how powerful the need is to resist any restriction of our personal freedoms.
When confronted by a demand or a command that curtails their freedom, people are motivated to restore their autonomy through a process called “psychological reactance.
Any time a leader makes a demand or commands what team members must do, they set off this psychological reactance.
Good leaders quickly learn that direction, instruction, suggestion, and recommendation produce far less noise and resistance than demand, command, and control.
Understanding the human motivation to react to anyone or anything that restricts our freedom is a central tenet of sound leadership.

t: The Fallacy of Composition and Judging True Character
q: The authentic self is displayed by what people do most often. Consistency is the key.
The Fallacy of Composition posits that people commonly infer what is true of a part must be true of the whole.
This fallacy is compounded by how good people are at impression-making.
They guard against the Fallacy of Composition by asking questions from several different angles, triangulating the data they collect, and observing people in as many different situations as possible.
The best leaders are slow to draw strong conclusions about character. They seek more direct experience with those they assess.

t: Teachers Love Theories
q: What makes these books so popular? One thing they do, I think it might be a characteristic of all world-beating ideas, is combine a big, explanatory theory with a few handy techniques that anybody can try.
Without theory this practical stuff would feel inert. Combine theory with practice, though, and it's magic.
There are tons of teachers whose use of BTC extends to almost nothing beyond these two practices. It's the "praising effort" of Liljedahl's approach.
The irony is that you need to go big and comprehensive if you want your small practical ideas to spread.
The big radical ideas get digested by the teaching profession until all that’s left are those catnip practices.
We need theories to help make sense of this mess. We want labels and categories and explanations to help us make order out of the chaos.
Look around at what resonates with people, there is a desperate, aching need for ideas, the bigger the better, and that's not going to change any time soon at all.

t: Making Good Decisions About Strategy
q: Research confirms that the leader and how they think about the future remain the most crucial components regarding the quality of a decision about strategy.
As it turns out, the best predictor of such a quality decision is whether a leader shapes a story about the future before they consider each option.
Like all good stories, this storyline includes key actors, their motivations, a set of actions and judgments that develop the narrative, and a conclusion with a lesson.
Stories are powerful organizing structures that enhance decision-making when they are deployed effectively.
Sound strategy starts with having a clear storyline that articulates a leader’s personal vision for the future.

t: First Weeks #2: What Are My Priorities in the Classroom? he-classroom/
q: I’d summarise your aim in the first week’s lessons like this: establish your expectations of student behaviour and expectations of student work in your classroom.

Instead of, or in addition to, having this talk about your expectations at the start of the year, look out for moments to demonstrate your expectations to the class. Show, don’t tell, as much as possible.
For instructions that will repeat, there’s merit to using the same language each time we share them.
I’ve seen lots of teachers introduce their expectations of student behaviour but I’ve rarely seen teachers introduce their expectation of student work.
If we want all the children to participate in every lesson, we want to make sure they're ready for it. You can practise just about every routine or act in the classroom.
If we let up on that expectation, students will notice and, perhaps subconsciously, adjust their behaviour.

t: 3-Read Friday #44: Routines, Priorities, and Theories
q: The start of the academic year is the ideal time to introduce or tighten up routines with students.
In this video from the Teach like a Champion team, we see two teachers discuss and then rehearse how they will introduce a routine for paired discussion (Turn and Talk) in their classrooms.
What will we focus on during the first few weeks of the new school year?
Pete aims this post at new teachers, but I think there is value here for teachers of all experiences.
Many readers will have heard about or read the book Building Thinking Classrooms by Peter Liljedahl.
In this post, Michael Pershan analyses why these books are so popular among teachers, and offers a few words of caution.

t: Talent May Be Portable But Success Is Not
q: In a world of fleeting organizational loyalty and remote work, the realization of how portable talent is has become top of mind for many leaders.
The idea that highly skilled team members can make a fast transition and apply their experience and knowledge in a new organization, however, is drastically overstated.
Worse yet, new colleagues are often looked at suspiciously once they land in an unfamiliar workplace.
Every organization has its secret doors and magic words that make life easier once you know them.
Research suggests that most top performers fail to reach the same level of success they enjoyed in the organization they recently left.

t: Moments of Genuine Connection (MGCs) Can Be EXHAUSTING
q: There is one skill that lies at the heart of any healthy person, family, school, community organization, or society: the ability to see someone else deeply and make them feel seen—to accurately know another person, to let them feel valued, heard, and understood.

Artificial intelligence is going to do many things for us in the decades ahead, and replace humans at many tasks, but one thing it will never be able to do is create person-to-person connections. If you want to thrive in the age of AI, you better become exceptionally good at connecting with others.
Seeing a student and then communicating that sight to students is a "skill"; it's "a powerfully creative act;" it involves the beaming of the light of my attention on a student.

Do you know how much work it takes to bring 133 new students into my mind and heart? To have them exist in my inner world, to attune myself to them, and to maintain a sense of self-possession as I do so? A LOT!

Most of us became teachers because we had a teacher or two who successfully MGCed with us. And much of the rest became teachers because they didn't receive enough of this stuff and wanted to make a change for future students.
But just because something appears simple does not mean it is easy. I'm telling you: this is work.

t: Clearing Up Misconceptions Of The Letter-Home Consequence
q: Done right, a thrice-misbehaving student must present and then articulate to their parents their rule-breaking behavior.
There are conditions that must be met. Otherwise, it can be a disaster. You could get angry complaints from parents, letters torn up and thrown away, and a visit from your administrator.
When I used the strategy for 12 years as an elementary teacher, I’d send a half dozen or so a year.
Another bad sign is if you don’t get a letter back. In every case, this because of one of the conditions above hasn’t been adequately met.
The most effective, honest, and responsible way to do this is to through a non-judgemental form letter the misbehaving but now contrite student must give their parents

t: Every Decision Has a Clock
q: Experienced leaders and decision-makers know that the timing of a decision can be as critical as the choice itself.
Every decision has an ideal window of time from which the advantages of the choice can be fully realized.
The best leaders don’t make a decision until they have to. They prize the optionality inherent in studying a problem and not acting on it until it is necessary.
Not surprisingly, the number one reason leaders make a poor decision is something they didn’t know.
The push and pull of keeping options open while not losing the opportunity to seize the moment is inherent in all good decision-making.

t: On Developing Leadership Character
q: Research over the last few decades has replaced the historic view of character as fixed and immutable to change with a more dynamic view of character dimensions that evolve over time.
Because character is actualized through behaviors and actions, practicing those behaviors can develop the personal qualities we most desire to improve.
The point not to miss is that character is formed and reformed through the practices of everyday life.
Character dimensions such as integrity, courage, temperance, collaboration, and accountability are tethered to specific actions and behaviors that bring them to light.
Great leaders engage in a host of specific behaviors every day. It’s time to start practicing some of them.

t: Influencing the Arc of Peoples Lives Without Knowing It
q: The power of leadership to influence the course of others’ lives goes far beyond enhancing job satisfaction and shaping careers.
Unnoticed at the time and typically unknown until decades later, some of the choices leaders make in the course of an average day can profoundly impact the very arc of people’s lives.
Contemplating the potential impact of their words, actions, and decisions —and the tremendous responsibility that entails — can be humbling for leaders.
Leaders who remember the powerful influence they wield often make better choices in the moment.
Many of the things you can count, don’t count. Many of the things you can’t count, really count.

t: The Terror of Taking Yourself Too Seriously
q: A serious and weighty approach to results is a tremendous asset when it is applied to the tasks at hand. But if that seriousness is allowed to corrupt the identity and self-image of the leader, it then becomes a huge liability.
Any time a leader begins to view themselves as an indispensable source of insight and wisdom, they stand on the cliff edge of self-worship.
Not surprisingly, they become frustrated and angry when people disagree with them or resist their views.
There is simply no good reason for you to allow the pursuit of success to color the way you see yourself.
As the English philosopher and critic G.K. Chesterton so aptly stated, “Angels can fly because they take themselves lightly.
